items.title: Strict rules for students in South Korea
items.text: South Korea is introducing strict anti-cheating measures ahead of its national college entrance exam, where over 500,000 students compete for scores that shape their future universities, careers, and social standing. The government’s crackdown follows a major scandal in which the top scorer of a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a hidden camera, a smartphone, and generative AI to obtain answers. Officials are now targeting smart glasses and hidden recording devices, deploying specially trained supervisors across 1,300 test sites to inspect students’ eye wear, and warning that cheaters face criminal prosecution. Despite intense academic pressure and calls to delay the test, the education ministry refused to postpone it. However, analysts doubt whether basic steps like blocking public Wi-Fi will stop tech-savvy cheaters, and note that expensive private tutoring already creates an uneven playing field in South Korea’s highly competitive education system. Difficult words: crackdown (severe action taken by authorities to stop illegal or unwanted behavior), tech-savvy (well-informed about or proficient in the use of modern technology, especially computers and digital devices), uneven (not equal, fair, or balanced in opportunity, quality, or distribution). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Strict rules for students in South Korea
items.text: South Korea is adding strict new rules to stop cheating during its national college entrance exam . More than 500,000 students take this important test, which decides their future universities and jobs. Recently, a major scandal happened when the top student in a national tax exam admitted to using a hidden camera and AI to find the right answers. Because of this, trained supervisors at 1,300 test centers will carefully check students’ glasses for hidden cameras before the exam begins. The education minister warned that anyone caught cheating with smart glasses will face serious legal punishment . Although the government refused to delay the test, experts question whether these rules will work and point out that expensive private schools already make the test unfair for poorer students. Difficult words: entrance exam (an examination a student must pass to get to a school, college, or university), scandal (an action which many people consider wrong and they are angry about it), punishment (a penalty for breaking a rule or law). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Strict rules for students in South Korea
items.text: More than 500,000 students in South Korea are taking a very big test to enter university. The test is very important for their future jobs and lives. Recently, someone cheats on another big exam. The man uses a small hidden camera and AI to get answers. Now, the government wants to stop cheating with smart glasses. Special workers will check students’ glasses at all test centers before the test starts. The government says that cheaters will get into big trouble with the police. Some experts think it is still hard to stop high-tech cheating. Also, the school system is already unfair. Rich people pay for better schools. These students do better on the test. Difficult words: enter (to come or get into a place or institution), hidden (when you keep something away from other people and they cannot see it), rich (when you have a lot of money). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is released worldwide
items.text: Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) has finally been released. Millions of video game fans worldwide are now playing it. They have waited 13 years for a new GTA game since the release of GTA 5. Gaming experts say the latest version could be the biggest entertainment release in history. It has already sold millions of copies, and it is set to make billions of dollars. Some fans are so excited that they are taking days off work or school to play it. An HR company in the UK said that workers in Britain booked around 83,000 days off because of the game. Many fans tried to make their games consoles think they lived in New Zealand by changing their region settings. They tried this so they could play the game earlier. GTA 6 has received excellent reviews for its high-quality, realistic graphics and exciting story. Players get to explore a huge world of crime and follow the lives of two criminals. However, many experts warn that the game is unsuitable for children under the age of 17. That is because it contains violence, killing, car theft, bad language, drugs, alcohol and sexual content. Media expert Jasmine Hood Miller said: "In GTA, players commit crimes, sometimes against ordinary people who did nothing wrong." She added: "GTA is a very well-made game that teens find fun to play." items.title: Wire upgrade at fault for grounding all US flights
items.text: Thousands of flights across the USA were grounded on Friday the 13th following a major communications failure in the country's air traffic control system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop after problems with radar and communications equipment. More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Thousands of flights were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded at airports nationwide. The problem was eventually traced to an overloaded router, possibly as a result of maintenance work to replace decades-old copper wires with fibre-optic cables. The FAA lifted the ground stop almost five hours later. Operations may take days to return to normal. The incident sparked widespread concern. Officials quickly reassured the public that it was not another 9/11. The US homeland security secretary said there had been no indication of a cyberattack or national security threat. He described the incident as a "telecommunications outage". Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the failure on outdated infrastructure. He said: "We have old switches and old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines." He added: "It's an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded." Duffy warned that systems would "continue to break" unless Congress allocated extra funds. He said: "I can't build things if I don't have money." items.title: France blames Iran for cyberattack on freezers
items.text: The French government has blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket freezers and refrigerators across France. The attacks happened last month. They hit around 700 supermarkets and shops. Hackers took control of the cooling systems in the fridges and freezers. Temperatures increased to more than 50 degrees Celsius. Thousands of tons of frozen food melted. Stores had to throw the food away because it was no longer safe to eat. The French Foreign Minister said the attack was on a level never seen before. France believes an Iranian cyber unit carried out the attack. Iran has strongly denied it was involved in the attacks and blamed the French government for them. Security experts have warned that cyberattacks could be more dangerous in the future. Similar attacks have already affected other European countries. A French blood bank has also been hit. Fortunately, workers stopped the blood products from being damaged. Cybersecurity expert Gerome Billois stated: "At the moment, they are attacking easy equipment, but we should be prepared to see attacks on other systems like water or electricity." Weak computer security can let hackers attack places and services, such as hospitals, airports, public transport and banks. This can put people's lives in danger. items.title: Chef fired for refusing to put pineapple on pizza
items.text: An Italian chef in Brisbane, Australia, has been fired for refusing to put pineapple on pizzas, among other reasons. He went to the Fair Work Commission to fight his dismissal, but failed to get his job back. The chef stated that topping pizzas with the tropical fruit was an "insult to his culture". He claimed he was sacked from a restaurant in May after repeatedly refusing his boss's instructions to make pineapple and ham pizzas for diners. His employer contended that the refusal was one of several workplace issues. The commission rejected the chef's application because it was submitted after the deadline. The chef has since found a job at another Italian restaurant. The question of whether pineapple belongs on pizza is a controversial one. It continues to divide public opinion. Pizza purists are aghast at the idea, but it is an established menu staple in many countries. The Hawaiian pizza was reportedly invented in Canada in 1962 after a chef used ham and pineapple as toppings. The restaurant owner expressed his opinion on it. He admitted that while the pizza was not his "absolute favourite," he would not "turn his nose up at it". Many restaurateurs insist that customers should be free to enjoy whatever ingredients and toppings they choose. Although the Hawaiian pizza is popular internationally, many Italians regard it as "culinary heresy". Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: Czechs protest to keep free TV and radio
items.text: Up to 400,000 people gathered at Letná Park in Prague, Czech Republic, on Sunday in what organizers call the largest demonstration since the 1989 Velvet Revolution. Protesters opposed Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’s government plan to abolish public license fees and fund Czech Television and Czech Radio directly from the state budget while cutting their funding by 15 percent. Critics and media experts warn that direct state financing gives politicians financial leverage over newsrooms and threatens editorial independence, and draw comparisons to government pressure on media in Hungary and Slovakia. The bill was pushed rapidly through parliament at 4:36 AM, just ahead of the November 17th anniversary, and it became a catalyst for wider anger against the ruling coalition’s approach to culture, defense, and democratic institutions. Babiš is facing intense public pressure, and he announced he would skip Velvet Revolution celebrations to ease tensions and signaled openness to a compromise funding model. Difficult words: abolish (to formally put an end to a system, practice, or institution), leverage (the power or ability to influence people, events, or decisions and get the outcome you want), catalyst (a person or event that quickly causes a big change or action). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Czechs protest to keep free TV and radio
items.text: Hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Prague, Czech Republic, to protest government plans to change how public media are paid for. Organizers said up to 400,000 citizens joined the protest, which was the biggest since 1989. Prime Minister’s government wants to end viewer license fees and pay for Czech Television and Czech Radio directly from the state budget, and also cut their money by 15 percent. Many people fear this change will let politicians control the news, similar to what happened in Hungary and Slovakia. The protest took place just before the Velvet Revolution anniversary and grew into a wider demonstration against the government. To calm the public, the Prime Minister said he would not attend the November 17 celebrations and suggested finding a compromise . Difficult words: citizen (a person who legally lives in a country), viewer license (an official payment required from people who own a television or radio to fund public broadcasting), compromise (an agreement reached by both sides). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Czechs protest to keep free TV and radio
items.text: Hundreds of thousands of people meet in a big park in Prague, the Czech Republic, on Sunday. They are angry about a new government plan for Czech TV and Czech Radio. The government wants to stop license fees and pay for TV and radio from state money. At the same time, they will get less money. Many people think that this will let politicians control the news and hurt freedom . Organizers say that it is the biggest protest in the country since 1989. To help calm people down, the Prime Minister says that he will not go to the November 17 holiday events. He wants to calm the situation and talk about a compromise . Difficult words: license fee (a monthly payment to support public television and radio), freedom (when you can do, say, and think what you want), compromise (solving a situation in a way where each side is happy). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Goosebumps
items.text: When we’re cold, watch a scary movie, or listen to our favorite song, we might get little bumps all over our skin. The bumps are called goosebumps; they are tiny muscles on our body that tighten our hair and make it stand upright. These bumps are an involuntary response to intense emotions. Goosebumps have a practical purpose for animals. When an animal’s hair sticks up, it makes the animal look bigger and helps protect it against predators. A raised layer of fur can also help keep an animal warm when cold. According to experts, goosebumps aren’t a survival reaction for humans. They are the result of an adrenaline rush sparked by an extreme emotion. Difficult words: involuntary (not done willingly or from choice), adrenaline (a hormone that the body makes from fear, anger, or excitement). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Goosebumps
items.text: Goosebumps are small bumps on our skin that appear when our hair stands up. We usually get goosebumps when we are scared, excited, or angry. Goosebumps are very useful for animals because they make them look bigger. Then the animals are safe from predators, which helps them survive . Also, the raised hair or fur keeps animals warm when it is cold. Experts say that people don’t need goosebumps to survive. Goosebumps happen when we are cold, watch a scary movie, or listen to our favorite song. An intense emotion, such as fear or anger, makes our body make more adrenaline. Adrenaline is a hormone which makes the heart beat faster, and it causes goosebumps. Difficult words: survive (to stay alive), fur (the short hair of some animals, for example, a rabbit), intense (very strong or great). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Goosebumps
items.text: Goosebumps are small bumps on our skin. They make our hair stand up. We get goosebumps when we are scared or angry. We get them when we watch a scary movie or listen to our favorite music. We get goosebumps when we are cold. Animals get goosebumps, too. They keep them safe. The animals look bigger. This situation saves them from predators . Raised hair or fur also keeps animals warm. Adrenaline causes goosebumps. Adrenaline is a chemical in the body. It makes the heart beat faster. The body usually makes it when in danger. People have more adrenaline when they experience a strong emotion . Difficult words: predator (an animal which eats other animals), fur (the short hair of some animals, for example, a rabbit), emotion (a strong feeling, for example, love or anger). items.title: A new device helps people with Tourette syndrome
items.text: A groundbreaking new wristwatch-style device developed through research at the University of Nottingham offers fresh hope for people living with Tourette syndrome and functional neurological disorders. The gadget works by sending gentle electrical stimulation via gel pad electrodes to the median nerve at the wrist, which connects to the brain and helps calm the neural activity responsible for involuntary tics. Clinical trials and early consumer feedback show that the device can substantially reduce tics and significantly improve patients’ quality of life. Users have reported being able to return to school, sleep better, and visit public places without fear. Thousands of devices have already been sold as a wellness product, while developers work toward securing medical regulatory approval to make it available on the NHS in the UK. Furthermore, early trials are exploring its potential to help individuals suffering from Parkinson’s disease, obsessive-compulsive disorder , and severe anxiety. Difficult words: involuntary (done without will or conscious control; happening automatically), substantially (to a great extent or degree; significantly), obsessive-compulsive disorder (a mental health disorder characterized by recurring, unwanted thoughts and repetitive behaviors). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: A new device helps people with Tourette syndrome
items.text: A new electronic device shaped like a smartwatch is helping teenagers who suffer from Tourette syndrome and sudden body tics . Created by researchers at the University of Nottingham, the gadget sends electrical signals to a nerve in the wrist. This signal travels to the brain and helps stop unpleasant movements very quickly. Many young patients say the device is life-changing because it allows them to go to school, sleep peacefully, and feel confident again. Thousands of people already bought the gadget as a wellness tool, and scientists hope it will soon be available through the National Health Service in the UK. Researchers are also testing if the same technology can help people with Parkinson’s disease and anxiety . Difficult words: tic (a contraction of the muscles, most often in the face or neck), life-changing (something what has a great effect on someone’s life), anxiety (a feeling of worry and nervousness). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
